children.text: What Are FHIR Implementation Guides?

FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is often called "the language of modern healthcare data," but a language alone is not enough. Two systems can both speak FHIR and still be unable to exchange data usefully if they use different resource structures, terminology codes, or workflow expectations. This is where Implementation Guides — IGs — come in. An IG is a formal, published specification that narrows the broad flexibility of FHIR into precise, agreed-upon rules for a specific use case. It defines which resources must be supported, which data fields are required versus optional, which code systems to use, and how the API calls should flow between systems.

HL7 International publishes FHIR IGs through a rigorous multi-stage process. A project team drafts the IG, submits it for community ballot as a "Standard for Trial Use" (STU), receives and reconciles hundreds of public comments from implementers, vendors, and regulators, and then publishes a revised version that reflects real-world feedback. Only after sustained, demonstrated implementation does a specification mature toward Normative status. This process ensures that IGs are not just theoretical documents — they are living standards shaped by the engineers, clinicians, and payers who actually build and operate systems against them.

Two HL7 FHIR Accelerator programs have produced the most influential IGs in the payer-provider space: the Da Vinci Project and the Gravity Project. An Accelerator is a structured program inside HL7 that brings together industry stakeholders to build and test IGs faster than the traditional standards process alone allows. Each Accelerator has a specific domain focus, a governing structure, and a commitment to testing in real pilots before declaring work complete.

body.analogy: Think of FHIR as the English language and an Implementation Guide as a legal contract written in English. Both parties understand the words, but the contract specifies exactly which terms mean what, what must be delivered by when, and what happens when something goes wrong. Without the contract, two fluent English speakers can still talk past each other.
body.concept: FHIR is flexible by design; IGs add the constraints that make interoperability precise and reliable.

children.text: The Da Vinci Project was founded in 2019 as an HL7 FHIR Accelerator with a specific mandate: accelerate FHIR adoption in value-based care by solving the most painful payer-provider data exchange problems. The project started with twenty-two founding member organizations and has grown to more than sixty industry-leading payers, providers, and health IT vendors. Its work is organized into use cases — discrete problem statements — each of which produces its own Implementation Guide and reference implementation. CMS's prior authorization interoperability mandates, finalized in the 2024 CMS-0057-F rule, cite Da Vinci IGs directly as the required technical standards.

The Gravity Project has a different origin and a different focus. It was initiated in November 2018 by the Social Interventions Research and Evaluation Network (SIREN) at the University of California, San Francisco, in collaboration with EMI Advisors LLC of Bethesda, Maryland. With initial funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, SIREN launched Gravity in 2019 as a national collaborative effort to develop structured data standards for social determinants of health (SDOH). Where Da Vinci attacks billing and authorization friction, Gravity attacks a different gap: the absence of standardized, machine-readable codes for the social conditions — food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers — that drive as much as 80 percent of health outcomes but are almost never documented in a form that clinical systems can act on.

children.text: Key Da Vinci IGs: PDex, PAS, CRD, and DTR

Da Vinci has published more than a dozen Implementation Guides. Four have become the centerpiece of federal interoperability mandates and real-world payer-provider integrations: the Payer Data Exchange IG (PDex), the Prior Authorization Support IG (PAS), the Coverage Requirements Discovery IG (CRD), and the Documentation Templates and Rules IG (DTR). Together these four IGs address the most administratively burdensome touchpoints in the American healthcare system: sharing a patient's longitudinal record when they switch payers, submitting and adjudicating prior authorization requests in near real-time, and ensuring that providers surface payer coverage rules inside their own EHR workflow before ordering a service.

The Payer Data Exchange IG (PDex), currently at version 2.1.0 (STU2.1) with version 2.2.0 in continuous development, defines the FHIR API surface that enables two critical data flows. First, payer-to-payer exchange: when a patient changes health plans, the new payer can call the old payer's PDex API to retrieve the patient's complete clinical history as FHIR resources conforming to US Core profiles. Second, payer-to-provider exchange: providers can call a payer's PDex endpoint to retrieve administrative and claims-derived clinical data about a patient, eliminating fax-based information requests. PDex has been updated to align with both US Core 6.1.0 and 7.0.0, enabling compliance with both CMS-0057-F and the ONC HTI-1 rule simultaneously.

The Prior Authorization Support IG (PAS), at version 2.1.0, defines a FHIR-based API workflow that replaces traditional X12 278 prior authorization transactions. Under PAS, a provider's EHR submits a FHIR Claim resource — bundled with all required supporting documentation — to the payer's PAS endpoint. The payer's system evaluates the request, potentially in real-time using clinical decision support, and returns a ClaimResponse resource. The entire round-trip can happen in seconds for straightforward cases, compared to the 72-hour or multi-day waits that characterize traditional PA processes. CMS-0057-F identifies PAS IG version STU 2.0.1 as the normative standard for the Prior Authorization API that covered payers must implement by January 1, 2027.

body.title: How the Da Vinci CRD + DTR + PAS Workflow Flows

children.text: Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), currently at version 2.1.0, is the upstream trigger in the Da Vinci burden-reduction workflow. It leverages CDS Hooks — a standard for embedding clinical decision support into EHR workflows — to allow payers to inject coverage information at the exact moment a clinician is making a treatment decision. CRD answers the question "Does this patient's plan require prior authorization for this service?" before the order is finalized, not after. This timing is critical: it is far more efficient to surface a coverage requirement during the ordering workflow than to discover a PA is needed only after a claim is denied.

Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), at version 2.1.0, is the companion to CRD. Where CRD identifies what is required, DTR provides the mechanism for gathering it. DTR uses SMART on FHIR to launch a payer-curated questionnaire application inside the provider's EHR. Using CQL (Clinical Quality Language) logic, the app queries the patient's FHIR records to pre-populate answers wherever the data already exists, surfacing only the truly missing information to the clinician. CMS has established its own Document Requirements Lookup Service (DRLS) — which combines CRD and DTR functionality — specifically for Medicare Fee-for-Service programs, validating the architecture at the federal level.

children.text: Da Vinci in Regulation: How CMS-0057-F Codified These IGs into Law

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule — formally CMS-0057-F — was published in January 2024 and represents the most consequential federal interoperability mandate since the 2020 CMS and ONC interoperability rules. The rule applies to Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges. Collectively, these plans cover the majority of Americans with government-sponsored or exchange-based coverage.

CMS-0057-F establishes a two-phase compliance timeline. The first phase took effect January 1, 2026: covered payers must now respond to standard prior authorization requests within 7 calendar days and to expedited requests within 72 hours; they must include specific, structured reasons for any denial; and they must begin publicly reporting prior authorization metrics, with the first annual reports due March 31, 2026 covering calendar year 2025 data. These provisions are not FHIR-specific — they are operational requirements that any payer must meet regardless of their technology approach. However, they create enormous pressure for automation, because manual PA processes cannot reliably meet 72-hour response windows at scale.

The second phase — and the one that directly references Da Vinci IGs — takes effect January 1, 2027. By that date, covered payers must have four FHIR-based APIs live and in production: a Patient Access API (based on PDex), a Provider Access API (also based on PDex), a Payer-to-Payer API (PDex again), and a Prior Authorization API based on Da Vinci PAS IG version STU 2.0.1. This is a landmark moment in U.S. healthcare standards history: for the first time, a specific named private-sector Implementation Guide — developed by a multi-stakeholder coalition, not a government body — is cited by name in a federal rule as a required technical standard. The Da Vinci Project's architecture has, in effect, become federal infrastructure.

CMS-0057-F requires covered payers to implement the Da Vinci PAS IG (STU 2.0.1) as the technical standard for their Prior Authorization API by January 1, 2027 — making Da Vinci specifications enforceable federal requirements for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and exchange plans.

The compliance landscape is challenging. Survey data from WEDI (Workgroup for Electronic Data Interchange) from late 2025 found that many payers were still in early stages of implementation for the Prior Authorization API specifically, with readiness varying widely across plan types and sizes. Smaller plans and state Medicaid agencies face particularly steep technical lift, as they may lack the internal engineering capacity to build FHIR API infrastructure from scratch. This has driven a cottage industry of FHIR platform vendors offering turnkey compliance solutions built on top of the Da Vinci specifications.

The regulation also reflects a broader policy strategy: rather than CMS building and mandating its own proprietary technology, the agency is leveraging privately developed, community-consensus standards that have already been tested in real implementations. This approach reduces the risk of government-mandated technology failures and creates a market-driven path to adoption — payers who implement Da Vinci IGs well will have a competitive compliance advantage, which accelerates the overall ecosystem. In mid-2025, more than fifty major health insurers voluntarily committed to targeting at least 80 percent real-time electronic prior authorization approval rates by 2027, reflecting the industry's recognition that FHIR-based PA is not just a regulatory requirement but a genuine operational efficiency driver.

body.content: Regence BlueCross BlueShield and MultiCare Connected Care became early proof that Da Vinci's architecture works at production scale. They launched what was described as the nation's first scalable FHIR-based prior authorization system using Da Vinci specifications. The results were dramatic: 94 percent of prior authorization inquiries received an immediate response — meaning the request was either approved or determined to require no PA at all — within seconds of submission. Clinicians at MultiCare could make requests directly from within their EHR, and the authorization decision flowed back into the same workflow without phone calls or faxes. At HIMSS 2025, MultiCare's Anna Taylor and Regence's Heidi Kriz presented this outcome as a benchmark for what standards-based prior authorization can achieve in practice.
body.title: Regence and MultiCare: The Nation's First Scalable FHIR Prior Authorization System

children.text: The Gravity Project: Putting Social Determinants of Health into FHIR

Social determinants of health — the conditions in which people are born, live, learn, work, and age — are estimated to drive 80 percent or more of health outcomes, yet they have historically been invisible to clinical information systems. A clinician might know that a patient's diabetes is poorly controlled, but unless food insecurity is documented in a structured, coded field, the health system has no way to connect that clinical problem to its social cause, refer the patient to a food pantry, or measure whether that referral reduced hospitalizations. The Gravity Project exists specifically to close that gap.

Gravity's approach is rigorous and consensus-driven. For each SDOH domain, a multi-stakeholder work group assembles the evidence base for how that condition should be defined, screened for, and documented. The group then works with SNOMED CT International, Regenstrief Institute (which stewards LOINC), and the ICD-10 Coordination and Maintenance Committee to create or curate the actual codes that represent each concept. This is painstaking work — getting a new concept into SNOMED CT or LOINC can take 12 to 18 months — but it ensures that Gravity's value sets are grounded in internationally recognized, maintained terminology systems rather than local codes that fragment data across organizations.

The Gravity SDOH Clinical Care Implementation Guide, currently at version 2.3.0 (STU 2.3, generated May 2025 and based on FHIR R4), defines FHIR profiles, value sets, and workflows for the full SDOH care cycle: screening a patient for social needs, documenting findings as FHIR Observations and Conditions, creating FHIR ServiceRequests for community referrals, and tracking the status of those referrals through FHIR Tasks. Version 3.0.0 is currently in ballot as of early 2026, with expanded domain coverage and improved alignment with the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI).

children.text: The SDOH domains covered by the Gravity IG span far beyond the two most commonly discussed. Food insecurity and housing instability were the first domains completed — the Gravity Project completed its initial food insecurity and housing data identification work before expanding. The current IG includes value sets and profiles for transportation insecurity, utility insecurity (inability to pay for heat, electricity, or water), educational attainment barriers, employment and financial strain, social isolation, intimate partner violence, and digital access barriers, among others. Each domain has a corresponding set of screening questions (mapped to LOINC panel codes), condition codes (mapped to SNOMED CT and ICD-10), and intervention codes for referrals.

State health systems and Medicaid programs are now formally recognizing Gravity standards. Washington State's 2025 FHIR Infrastructure Roadmap named the Gravity SDOH Clinical Care IG as a core interoperability standard for community and clinical data exchange. New York sought to leverage Gravity standards for exchange of SDOH screenings between clinical systems and community-based organizations like Unite Us and FindHelp, ensuring that FHIR-compliant screenings could be ingested by social care platforms in real-time. Colorado's vendor contracts for its statewide social care platform explicitly require Gravity-aligned terminology and FHIR-based exchange. These state-level mandates are creating the network effects that transform a voluntary standard into a de facto requirement.

body.content: A patient comes in for a diabetes follow-up. The nurse administers the LOINC-coded AHC HRSN screening panel (LOINC panel code 96777-8) inside the EHR. The patient screens positive for food insecurity. The EHR creates a FHIR Observation with LOINC code 88122-7 ("Within the past 12 months, we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more") and a FHIR Condition with SNOMED CT code 733423003 ("Food insecurity"). The care coordinator creates a FHIR ServiceRequest for a food pantry referral, which is transmitted via Task to the community-based organization's FHIR endpoint. When the referral is fulfilled, the CBO updates the Task status, and the EHR receives a structured confirmation — all without a fax machine or a phone call.
body.title: How Gravity Codes Flow Through a Real Care Encounter

children.text: Implementation Reality: Adoption, Challenges, and What Comes Next

Real-world adoption of both Da Vinci and Gravity IGs is accelerating but uneven. On the Da Vinci side, the Regence-MultiCare prior authorization pilot is no longer an outlier — it is a benchmark. The Da Vinci Trebuchet pilot program organizes multi-organization cohorts to test specific IGs in production environments, with 2026 cohorts already forming. CMS's regulatory deadline of January 1, 2027 for FHIR-based PA APIs is creating real urgency across the industry. Roughly 65 percent of EHR transactions on Epic systems achieved electronic prior authorization by 2025, with ePA transaction volumes nearly doubling from 2023 to early 2025.

The barriers to full PAS IG adoption are real and multi-layered. Technical complexity is one factor — implementing a compliant FHIR Claim submission endpoint that correctly handles all PAS workflow states (pended, approved, denied, modified) requires significant engineering investment. Organizational alignment is another: the PAS workflow requires both the EHR vendor and the payer platform to implement complementary sides of the same API, which means bilateral negotiations that take time. Smaller regional health plans and safety-net providers face resource constraints that make in-house implementation difficult. And despite a January 2027 deadline, WEDI's 2025 surveys found that a meaningful share of covered entities had not yet begun implementation work for the Prior Authorization API specifically.

ONC has provided an important tool to support PAS adoption: the Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support Test Kit, launched on Inferno (the federal FHIR testing platform). This test kit allows implementers to validate their PAS implementations against the IG's conformance requirements before going live, reducing the risk of interoperability failures in production. The existence of an authoritative, publicly available test kit is a meaningful maturity signal — it means the IG has progressed from specification to executable, testable infrastructure.

body.message: CMS-0057-F's January 1, 2027 API implementation deadline applies to Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, CHIP managed care, and exchange plans. Plans that fail to meet requirements face potential compliance action. The prior authorization operational requirements (72-hour expedited, 7-day standard response) already took effect January 1, 2026. Organizations that have not begun their Da Vinci PAS implementation should treat this as an urgent priority, not a future concern.
body.title: The 2027 Deadline Is Not a Soft Target

children.text: On the Gravity side, the implementation picture is more heterogeneous. Major EHR platforms including Epic have built SDOH screening and documentation modules that align with Gravity value sets, making it easier for health systems to capture structured SDOH data. But the harder problem — closing the referral loop with community-based organizations — remains a work in progress. CBOs typically lack the technical capacity to build FHIR endpoints, so interoperability between clinical systems and the social care sector depends on intermediary platforms like Unite Us, FindHelp, and Aunt Bertha that can translate between FHIR and the APIs those organizations actually use. States like New York and Colorado are addressing this through explicit vendor contract requirements, creating the contractual obligation that drives technical investment.

Looking ahead, both projects have substantial roadmaps. Da Vinci is expanding into clinical data exchange between providers and payers for value-based care performance measurement, and is developing IGs for attachments — the structured clinical documents that support claims adjudication. Gravity is developing version 3.0 of its SDOH Clinical Care IG with expanded domain coverage and is pursuing deeper integration with the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) — the federally required minimum dataset for EHR certification. As SDOH data elements enter USCDI and EHR certification criteria, Gravity's approach shifts from voluntary best practice to the floor that every certified EHR must support. That normative shift, once complete, will make structured social needs documentation as routine as recording a blood pressure.

This API must be live and in production at covered payers — including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, CHIP managed care, and exchange plans — by January 1, 2027. This makes PAS IG STU 2.0.1 one of the only privately developed, multi-stakeholder FHIR Implementation Guides to be formally mandated in a U.S. federal rule.
